newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik leaders demand end to fighting, blame mafia.
newsitem.headline: Tajik leaders demand end to fighting, blame mafia.

text.p: Fighting in the Tajik capital Dushanbe died down on Sunday after an armed group seized a northern district from a rival warlord.
Russian news agencies said fighting which erupted on Saturday continued in a region south of Dushanbe, but journalists could not reach the area to confirm the reports.
President Imomali Rakhmonov, struggling to keep order just weeks after signing an agreement ending four years of civil war, summoned Tajikistan's Security Council.
It ordered the rivals to stop fighting within three days or face "destruction". Rakhmonov blamed the violence on mafia-style criminal gangs who were not interested in peace.

"The people who provoke these military clashes are connected with the economic mafia, the drugs mafia and the criminal world," he was quoted as saying in a statement issued after the Security Council meeting.

War and instability in Tajikistan, a mountainous country of 5.7 million, have left the republic carved up into independent fiefdoms controlled by a bewildering array of maverick armed groups similar to those in neighbouring Afghanistan.

In northern Dushanbe, this correspondent saw fighters in green bandanas clebrating their control of the area by waving assault rifles and making jubilant war-cries as they careered around in private cars and on army trucks.

A mangled white pick-up truck hit by a rocket and several burned-out homes testified to Saturday's fighting in the district, centring around a cement factory. Few civilians braved the streets and bazaars were deserted.
"People can't work, people can't go about their business peacefully," said Narzalo Tiloyev, 27, an accountant waiting in vain by the side of the road for transport out of the district.
"It was hard before but now it's even harder".

The victorious men of Sukhrob Kasimov, an Interior Ministry commander, and those of defeated Yakub Salimov, a senior customs official and former interior minister, are nominally loyal to President Rakhmonov's shaky government.
They have no link to the former Soviet republic's armed Islamic opposition, which signed the peace accord with the government in June intended to end the civil war.
The government and the opposition had begun a tentative share-out of power and a truce has held broadly since December.
Fighting flared over the killing of Kasimov's uncle. But Western diplomats said tanks and rockets had been used not just to settle a family feud but as part of a battle for turf.
Russian news agencies reported a second day of heavy fighting between two other rival groups in the Fakhrobad Valley about 30 km (20 miles) south of Dushanbe.

Reporters were stopped at a checkpoint just south of Dushanbe and prevented from going any further. The checkpoint commander said fighting was continuing between the presidential guard and a force led by a maverick government commander, Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev.
"We are still fighting Khudoyberdyev. He wants to take the city," he said.
Khudoyberdyev, who has mutinied twice and is seen as a potential coup-maker, had wanted Kasimov to leave the capital.
But the new fighting threatened anarchy in the tense capital, ringed by parched biscuit-coloured mountains.
"There's been a complete breakdown in law and order," said a Western aid worker. "The government looks very weak."
Rakhmonov is likely to look to a predominantly Russian force of Commonwealth of Independent States peacekeepers to shore up his grip on power -- although its mandate ran out last month.
About 20,000 Russian troops are carrying out peacekeeping duties and guarding borders in Tajikistan.
The U.S. embassy has advised all its citizens to stay indoors.
There was no word on casualties, but the International Committee of the Red Cross said on Saturday it had supplied a Dushanbe hospital with medicines to treat 40 injured people.
